newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel deal crunch for ferries too.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel deal crunch for ferries too.

text.p: Eurotunnel's debt deal may have helped it back from the brink of ruin, after a year of financial uncertainty, but its arch rivals the Channel ferry lines warned on Wednesday the move was fundamental to their future too.
The Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator said it had broken the deadlock over its 9.0 billion pound ($14 billion) debt late on Tuesday and agreed broad rescue terms with its lead bankers.
But details are not due to be released until next week.
The ferry companies, which have been waging a cut-throat price war for market share on routes across the English Channel, said the impact on the industry would depended on those details.

A spokesman for Swedish ferry giant Stena Line, which runs a fleet of roll-on roll-off ferries and catamarans between Britain and France, told Reuters on Wednesday, "The restructuring effect will be fundamental to Eurotunnel and to us. But we are waiting for the details.
"This is a major competitor with massive influence in the market -- we are therefore acutely interested in its restructuring," he added.

So far, Eurotunnel has been winning the offensive for market share, carving out 45 percent of the cross Channel market to make it the biggest of all operators, ahead of the largest ferry line Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O).
Eurotunnel's market share soared after it slashed its duty free and ticket prices in May, with the economy vehicle fares for its Le Shuttle services being cut by more than 50 percent.

Passenger numbers through the tunnel were further boosted by a changeover in ownership of the Eurostar passenger service trains which run through the tunnel. Eurotunnel is paid a fee based on the level of this train traffic.

The new owners, a consortium including Virgin Airlines and coach operator National Express, have marketed Eurostar more aggressively, as an alternative not just to ferries but also to short-haul continental flights.
Industry analysts said Eurotunnel was clearly winning the market share war despite its precarious financial position.

Michael Cohen, analyst at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters he saw Eurotunnel's share continuing its rise. "I think we may see further improvement -- perhaps to close to 60 percent. But Eurotunnel will have to reach a balance on sales and prices."
Selwyn Jones, analyst at Credit Lyonnaid Laing also said "Prices cannot possibly go on at this level."
Stena agreed that the current pricing levels were unsustainable, especially for Eurotunnel itself.

"Eurotunnel has the biggest market share but is losing millions and millions of pounds a day. It has grown its share tremendously but there must be pressure on Eurotunnel to get prices up again - when you consider its debt levels," said the ferry company spokesman.

Analysts said that for Eurotunnel to survive and thrive at least half its debt must be dealt with in some way -- and this is exactly where the restructuring package is expected to help, switching about half of it into equity, according to insiders.
Eurotunnel faces the added urgency that rivals like P&O and Stena are already exploring possible link-ups in an attempt to cut excess capacity and boost their profits.

This in turn would create a more formidable competitor than Eurotunnel has seen to date, though analysts predict any large-scale plan to combine fleets would face intense regulatory and trade union scrutiny and possibly opposition. ($1=.6385 Pound)
